extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mass communication/journalism; media professionals and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate organizational- and extramedia-level factors that shape news content (ownership type, internal control mechanisms, source selection, etc.) and how they affect what gets reported and how. Used for media studies analyses, content analyses, and assessments of newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership type (independent vs chain) affects content
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain ownership (versus independent ownership) usually implies absentee ownership and may lead to organizational imperatives outweighing local community concerns; ownership type correlates with differences in tone, slant, and priorities of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: group-owned stations may broadcast more news (Wirth & Wollert, 1976); studies show both positive and negative effects of chain ownership (Hale, 1988). Example: Knoxville Journal became more favorable toward a local World's Fair after Gannett takeover (Browning et al., 1984). Assess whether local emphasis, editorial slant, and hiring practices shift after ownership changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee socialization / organizational role orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees at independent papers are socialized to the single local organization, while chain-paper employees are also socialized to the larger chain, reducing prominence of community role expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: measure reporters' and editors' community attachments and role perceptions. Parsons et al. (1988) found community role expectations are reduced in chain papers and conflict resolved in favor of the organization. Look for indicators such as job mobility, career paths within chains, and expressed loyalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership effects on allocation of reporting resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain takeovers may increase ad/subscription rates, reduce expensive 'serious' news gathering, and lead to hiring less qualified journalists (Bagdikian, 1987), but can also standardize product and bring capital/resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate changes in news hole size, staffing qualifications, proportion of space devoted to news/editorial/features, and investment in investigative reporting pre/post ownership change. Note mixed empirical findings; some chains infuse capital and industry standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and local conflict coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally owned or in-state owned papers devote more space to reporting local community conflict than out-of-state chain-owned papers; ownership geography matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donohue, Olien, & Tichenor (1985): in-state/local ownership showed three times the space to local conflict. Track coverage levels of local government conflict over time and by ownership status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership effects on editorial content and partisan endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain newspapers publish fewer argumentative, local, or controversial editorials and are more likely to endorse presidential candidates; chain papers show de facto homogeneity in endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thrift (1977) found fewer argumentative/local/controversial editorials in chains. Examine editorial counts/types and endorsement patterns (St. Dizier, 1986; Wackman et al., 1975) to evaluate partisan convergence and intra-chain uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ownership and media diversity/comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies owning both newspapers and broadcast outlets (cross-ownership) raise concerns about media diversity because one company may control multiple community outlets; cross-owned outlets may transmit as much or more news but communities with single-company ownership have less comprehensive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare news breadth and public affairs content in markets with cross-ownership vs multiple owners (Wirth & Wollert, 1976; Stempel, 1973). Look for evidence of news-value transfer from newspapers to broadcast counterparts (Wollert, 1978).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational control hierarchy (who exercises power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is exercised through hierarchical relationships (owners → publishers → editors → reporters); organizations must socialize and enforce routines and policies to maintain conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess formal and informal lines of authority and how decisions cascade. Consider when top management intervenes (high stakes) versus routine delegation, and where boundaries of acceptability are communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt policy directives and memos as direct control
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations sometimes use explicit policy guidelines or memos to dictate content decisions (e.g., a memo urging staff to consider community conservatism when covering a homosexual-rights rally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify written/explicit policies and directives that instruct story/photo/cutline/headline selection. Evaluate frequency and impact of such overt interventions versus subtler controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control via reward and punishment systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Most control is accomplished through rewards (promotions, raises, scoops, bylines, access) for conformity and punishments (demotion, firing, killing stories) for nonconformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure career outcomes, access to sources, and assignments as incentives. Note that 'killing' stories or blue-penciling functions as a powerful deterrent and can produce self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto control through routines, socialization, and guessing supervisors' preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine newsgathering practices and the covert 'consistent orientation' of an organization lead reporters to deduce supervisors' wants and self-select or shape content accordingly; control often occurs without visible interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unwritten norms, internal house organs, and informal cues that teach reporters what is acceptable. Breed (1955) emphasizes covert policy maintained through such mechanisms; journalists may internalize these standards leading to conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breed's social-control mechanisms (blue-penciling, killing stories, covert policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy is maintained not by formal rules but by covert consistent orientation; mechanisms include editorial blue‑penciling, changing stories with extraneous reasons given (time/space), and letting policy remain undiscussed and unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances of editing that remove or alter objectionable material, the stated reasons given, and the role of internal communications in maintaining covert policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational pressures for conformity (remoteness and bureaucracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of top editors is enhanced by remoteness, layers of bureaucracy, and the lack of need to justify decisions, forcing underlings to guess what will please or displease them (Gans, 1979).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate organizational structure, distance between decision-makers and reporters, and transparency in decision rationale. These structural features predict higher self-censorship and conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards for aligning with institutional interests vs penalties for threatening them
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters who best reflect institutional interests receive scoops, access, reputation; those who threaten institutional interests are marginalized—fostering self-censorship and selective reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace access patterns, beat privileges, and recognition. Examine cases of journalists who reported against institutional interests and subsequent career effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of newsroom workforce and limits of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A more diverse workforce may improve media reflection of a multicultural society, but minority journalists often adapt to dominant organizational culture, with constrained ability to change portrayals; they may be told their stories 'lack newsworthiness' or dropped for space/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representation at different organizational levels and whether minority journalists' story proposals are accepted, altered, or dropped. Consider Jill Nelson's insights and Wilson & Gutierrez (1985) findings on adaptation pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational-level summary: economic goals and conglomerate conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations' primary goal (economic profit) and their structure influence content via occupational culture, independence from larger corporate enterprises, hiring/promotion, and self-censorship; conglomerate complexity increases potential conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ownership structures, profit imperatives, inter-unit effects within conglomerates, and policies addressing conflicts of interest. Evaluate how economic pressures shape editorial priorities and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources as extramedia influences: availability, perspective, and information subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources (other journalists, eyewitnesses, officials, organizations, advocates) provide differing points of view and information; journalists must sift conflicting inputs to create accurate and complete reports. Organizations often provide 'information subsidies' that are easier/cheaper to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the range of sources used in coverage and note which provide packaged, timely materials (press releases, briefings). Evaluate reliance on information subsidies and the effect on framing and content completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source manipulation: withholding, lying, and deliberate misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources may withhold information or mislead journalists; deliberate misinformation can be supplied (e.g., attorney admitting to misleading reporters), and journalists' hunger for information can facilitate coverage of 'nothing' stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess verification practices, cross-checking, and use of corroborating evidence. Consider ethical implications and incidences of being misled (case examples: Amy Fisher trial attorney comment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of official/organizational sources due to availability and perceived authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often rely on official sources (government, police) because they are available, perceived as having important things to say, and make verification efficient; police provide a steady stream of usable crime information with vested interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate source mix and the proportion of official vs independent/technical sources. Recognize that official-source dominance can skew causes/solutions toward institutional perspectives (Paletz & Entman, Gandy, Sherizen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Event type, deadlines, proximity, and media type shape source selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of event (human-interest vs issue), time pressure (wire services), geographic distance, and medium (print vs broadcast) influence whether individual or organizational/official sources are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical patterns: Atwater & Green (1988) — human-interest hijacking coverage used many individuals; Seo (1988) — individuals covered when available; Fico (1984a/b) — part-time legislatures elicit fewer sources; Martin (1988) — distant outlets rely more on official sources. Incorporate event and operational constraints into source-evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential sources and motivations for anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some official sources provide information anonymously ('a high government source') to test ideas, provide background, or for personal satisfaction/benefit; journalists must balance public interest and source protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reasons for confidential sourcing, evaluate corroboration standards required before publishing, and examine potential incentives sources have for leaking background information (Gassaway).
